title: The Verse of Repentance
speaker: Myoki Raizelah Bayen
summary: In this dharma talk, the main teaching is that true repentance involves acknowledging and taking responsibility for our own and others' suffering caused by greed, hate, and delusion - the fundamental causes of our conditioned self. It's not just about apologizing or feeling remorse, but rather about embracing the regret, grief, and sorrow that arises from recognizing our interconnectedness with all beings. This requires a non-judgmental and open-hearted approach, acknowledging our humanness and the imperfections that come with it, while also taking full responsibility for our actions and their impact on others.

sentences.text: So, I first want to apologize.
I didn't expect to be giving a dharma talk tonight; Tim has a little tummy bug, so I am breaking the Dogen pattern.
Because I didn't have advance notice, I'm recycling a dharma talk that I wrote for a different occasion, so I'm sorry.
I want to invite you to join me in chanting the verse of repentance, which is on the top of page four.
I'd like to say that together three times.
And really, as you say the words, bring your attention to your body and how it feels in your body to say these words.
Let them wash through you.
Right?
So, it's not just words on a page, but something coming from you and also within you.
Powerful words, aren't they?
My teacher said, make them your mantra.

Pat Phelan, abbess of the Chapel Hill Zen Center in North Carolina, says in this verse we acknowledge our endless and beginninglessness, our inexhaustible delusion which propels us into birth and death.
This is the line that stands out to me from beginningless, beginningless greed, hate, and delusion.
What does that mean?
All of the greed, hate, and delusion that came before me, and it would mean also all that follows me.

All the innumerable causes and conditions from the beginningless beginning of time that create the greed, hate, and delusion that I embody and all the seeds of greed, hate, and delusion that I plant through my unwholesome thoughts, words, and actions I now fully avow.
Mine and everyone's.
The greed, hate, and delusion of the whole world.
Wow.
I've often asked myself, how do I save all beings?
How do I repent for all beings?
How do I repent for all beings?
And what is repentance anyway?
So I looked it up in the dictionary, and this is what the dictionary says: the action of repenting, sincere regret or remorse for something wrong that you have done.
Vow means to assert or confess openly.
So here it is, my confession, all my ancient twisted karma, and all the ancient twisted karma of everyone who came before me and after me.
I now fully vow.
That is, I acknowledge with regret, grief, sorrow, the wrongdoing of all living beings before me and after me.
What is it like to really embrace and fully feel that regret, grief, and sorrow for the wrongdoing of all living beings?
What is it like for you to fully feel the grief, regret, and sorrow for all living beings?
It's kind of mind blowing.
When I first started to work with this verse, taking it on as a mantra, I felt truly sad.
I have hurt others, sometimes people close to me, sometimes those that I love.
I've taken what is not mine.
I've been dishonest with myself and others.
I've been selfish time and time again, endlessly.
And just as all those who came before me in greed, hate, and delusion planted seeds for my greed, hate, and delusion, well, I have planted seeds for those that come after me.
One of my biggest regrets is how critical and blaming I was in my relationship with my ex-husband.
I grew up in a fairly harsh, critical household.
My mother was a perfectionist who communicated in so many ways that I was not good enough.
And my father's need for control led him to continual condescension in his attitude and his actions.
When I am unhappy or dissatisfied with an aspect of my life, when things are not going as I would like, my knee-jerk reaction is to blame and criticize.
It may sound like it, but I'm not blaming my parents.
But this is my conditioned response.
And I know I have to take full responsibility for every single time I hurt someone by being blaming or critical.
I was unhappy and dissatisfied in my first marriage.
My knee-jerk reaction was to blame and criticize.
That came up more times than I'd like to admit.
So in working with this verse in recent weeks, it became clear to me that my ex-husband deserves my deepest apology.
I'm sorry.
So I wrote him an email to deliver my apology.

I don't know if he forgives me, but it opened the door to forgiveness in myself, for myself, acknowledging my own humanness, the karmic, deluded self, being a karmic, deluded self, the separate self, protecting the separate self, all of my ancient twisted karma.
In his book, *Returning to Silence*, Katagiri Roshi said that repentance in Buddhism means perfect openness of heart.
My experience in writing that letter of apology to my ex-husband did open my heart to forgiveness.
In Reb Anderson's book, *Being Upright*, he delineates between two types of repentance.
The first is formal repentance, formally acknowledging to another person that you've done harm, maybe with an apology, a feeling of regret for your unwholesome action.
That was what that letter was to my ex-husband, a formal repentance.
And then Reb says there's formless repentance.
This refers to the non-dual or the absolute perspective.
Formless repentance is for any self-centered act, any thought, speech, or action motivated by the separate self which serves to solidify the separate self.
I ask, isn't that the main preoccupation with our ego, our separate self?
For me, I believe it is.
I pour a tremendous amount of energy into reinforcing my conditioned self and all the identities it includes.
I'm continually trying to protect myself, protect my needs, make myself heard, make myself understood, assert myself, preserve my sense of self.
Can you relate?
This seems to be the main job of the conditioned self.
The karmic self by nature is completely self-centered, maybe even needy and greedy at times.
And this is what it means to be human.
Each of us has a conditioned self.
There's no escaping it.
So getting back to the dictionary definition, repentance can't be remorse for wrongdoing.
We haven't done anything wrong by being born a human.
Self-centered activity comes with the territory.
So as I worked with the verse of repentance, I came to feel it more as a verse of acknowledgement.
All my ancient twisted karma from beginningless greed, hate, and delusion, born through body, speech, and mind, I now fully avow.
An acknowledgement of our humanness.
But being human is no excuse.
We still need to be fully responsible for the actions we take.
Saying I'm sorry matters.
It acknowledges that we're connected.
What we think, say, and do affects others.
Reb Anderson says, practicing confession reawakens the heart of compassion and the appreciation of others.

So I'd like to invite us to say it together again: *All my ancient twisted karma from beginningless greed, hate, and delusion, born through body, speech, and mind, I now fully avow.* Thank you for listening.
We have lots of time for, let's see, do we have groups of three?
I'd like for us to get into groups of three.
Each person can have five minutes to do a monologue.
If you run out of things to say, that's absolutely fine.
We are all really good at sitting quietly until I ring the bell and it's the next person's turn.
And that quiet time is just as important as the time, if not more, that you spend speaking.
Because it's in the quiet time that sometimes the unexpected emerges.
Something bubbles up that you didn't plan on saying, that you didn't pre-rehearse when the other person was talking, or think about ahead of time.
And that's when the unknown is uncovered.
So I've heard a lot of different reactions to doing these triads and dyads because some people feel uncomfortable.

Actually, most people do, and I want to say that it's meant to be uncomfortable because any time we let ourselves step into the unknown, any time we let what's not yet discovered about the self reveal itself, it can be uncomfortable.
And it's sort of meant to set you up for that.
And it's not to say that that's what has to happen.
There is no right or wrong.
There is no how it should or shouldn't be.
But I would invite you to meet your discomfort if it's uncomfortable and maybe that's what you find yourself talking about.
If that's what's there, that's what's there.
But I have a question for you anyway.
Think about something that you've done that was hurtful or unwholesome sometime when maybe you hurt someone or you felt like you did something wrong, regretful.
And as you think about that instance, was it something that was a habitual or conditioned response?
Was it something rooted in protecting yourself, your sense of self?
And notice how you feel when you recount your actions.
What would repentance look like for you?
